plan.contextChunk:
property: conditional on $x_2$, variable $x_3$ is independent of
variable $x_1$. The joint probability of all the variables shown here is
$p(x_1, x_2, x_3, y_1, y_2, y_3) =  \phi_{12}(x_1, x_2)  \phi_{23}(x_2, x_3)
\psi_{1}(y_1, x_1) \psi_{2}(y_2, x_2) \psi_{3}(y_3, x_3)$. Using
$p(a,b) = p(a \bigm | b) p(b)$, we can also write the probability of the
$x$ variables conditioned on the observations $y$,
$$p(x_1, x_2, x_3 \bigm | y_1, y_2, y_3) =  
\frac{1}{p(\mathbf{y})} \phi_{12}(x_1, x_2)  \phi_{23}(x_2, x_3) \psi_{1}(y_1, x_1) \psi_{2}(y_2, x_2) \psi_{3}(y_3, x_3).$$
For brevity, we write $p(\mathbf{y})$ for $p(y_1, y_2, y_3)$. Thus, to
form the conditional distribution, within a normalization factor, we
simply include the observed variable values into the joint probability.
For vision applications, we often use such Markov chain structures to
describe events over time.

To capture relationships over space, a two-dimensional (2D) structure is
useful, called a **Markov random field** (MRF) @Blake2011:

![Two-dimensional Markov random field.](figures/graphical_models/mrf.png){width="48%" #fig-leafs}

Then the joint probability over all the variables factorizes into this
product: 

$$p(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{y}) = 
\frac{1}{p(\mathbf{y})}
\prod_{(i,j)} \phi_{ij}(x_i, x_j) \prod_i \psi_i(x_i, y_i),$$
where the first product is over all spatial neighbors $i$ and $j$, and the second
product is over all nodes $i$.

An example of how Markov random field models are applied to images is
depicted in @fig-leafs, which show a small image region and its context
in the image (@fig-leafs [a]). @fig-leafs [b] shows an MRF with each
node corresponding to a pixel of the image region. The states of an MRF
can be indicator variables of image segment membership for each pixel.
The states of a hypothetical most-probable configuration of this MRF are
shown as the color of each node in this illustration.

:::{#fig-leafs layout-ncol="2"}
![](figures/graphical_models/leaf2.jpg){width=97% #fig-leafs-a}

![](figures/graphical_models/leaf1.jpg){width=100% #fig-leafs-b}

Fig (a) Image to be segmented and a local region of (a) marked in red.  (b) Visualization of an MRF of nodes corresponding to image pixels inside the marked region, with states indicating segment membership, for a hypothetical most probable configuration.
::: 

## Directed Graphical Models

In addition to undirected graphical models, another type of graphical
model is commonly used. **Directed graphical models** @Koller2009
describe factorizations of the joint probability into products of
conditional probability distributions. Each node in a directed graph
contributes a well-specified factor in the joint probability: the
probability of its variable, conditioned on all the variables originating
arrows pointing into it. So this graph

![A directed graphical model with three variables.](figures/graphical_models/directed.png){width="20%" #eq-directedjoint}

denotes the joint probability,

elements: 3x3 grid of hidden state nodes (x_ij) represented as spheres on a base plane, initially white
3x3 grid of observation nodes (y_ij) represented as gray/colored spheres elevated vertically above each x_ij
horizontal/lateral connecting cylinders (edges) between neighboring hidden state nodes (representing spatial potentials phi_ij)
vertical connecting cylinders between each hidden state node x_ij and its observation y_ij (representing local evidence potentials psi_i)
floating text labels 'x1', 'x2', 'x3' and 'y1', 'y2', 'y3' matching the back row of nodes in the original diagram
visual highlight ring/halo for indicating the Markov Blanket when a node is selected

interactions.label: Spatial Coupling (phi)
interactions.teaches: Higher spatial coupling forces neighboring hidden states to agree, smoothing out noisy local observations.

interactions.label: Observation Noise
interactions.teaches: Controls how noisy the upper observed nodes (y) are relative to the true underlying segmentation pattern.

interactions.label: Select Node
interactions.teaches: Click any hidden node x to highlight its Markov blanket—the set of nodes that, when observed, conditionally isolate it from the rest of the graph.

demo_steps.title: Hidden vs. Observed States
demo_steps.narration: In a Markov Random Field (MRF), the bottom layer contains the hidden true states (x), while the top layer contains the noisy observations (y). Each vertical link represents the likelihood potential psi_i connecting a pixel's observation to its actual state.

demo_steps.title: Denoising via Spatial Coupling
demo_steps.narration: When observation noise is high, the data layer (y) becomes corrupted. By turning up the spatial coupling (phi), the horizontal links force neighboring hidden nodes to coordinate, filtering out local noise and producing a clean, segmented region.

demo_steps.title: The Markov Blanket
demo_steps.narration: Click on the center node x2. Notice how its immediate neighbors (the adjacent x nodes and its own y node) light up. This is its Markov blanket: conditioned on these specific neighbors, this node is entirely independent of all other nodes in the network.

interactionPlan.camera_suggestion: An elevated 3D oblique angle looking down from the front-left, clearly showing the 2D grid floor, the vertical stems, and the floating observation layer.
interactionPlan.view_reasoning: (1) The grid lines of the MRF run horizontally left-to-right and diagonally receding into the page to the upper-right. (2) This receding diagonal structure implies a camera azimuth rotated away from a flat front view, specifically looking from the front-left (around -30 to -45 degrees). (3) The vertical offset of the y-nodes relative to the x-nodes is prominent, showing a clear height gap that requires a moderate, shallow elevation angle of around 20 to 25 degrees to avoid compressing the vertical stems too much.

camera_view.view_notes: Maintains the distinct spatial layered look of the MRF where x and y nodes do not overlap vertically from this viewpoint.

True state is a binary segmentation (e.g., a diagonal edge of colored nodes); observations y are noisy versions of this.

evaluation.geometry_accuracy_analysis: The 3D grid structure accurately reconstructs the 3x3 MRF graph with correct topology (3x3 base grid of hidden nodes, each vertically connected to an observed node). It uses real 3D primitives (spheres, cylinders) and includes interactive halos. Viewpoint and perspective align well with the source layout, though the node label mapping (x1, x2, x3) is slightly misaligned relative to the source diagram's straight-column indexing.
evaluation.geometry_accuracy_improvement: Align the node labels (x1, x2, x3) directly to the columns along the same primary axis as shown in the source figure, rather than skewed across diagonal depth axes.
evaluation.interactivity_usability_analysis: The developer implemented several high-quality, pedagogically rich interactions: (1) A 'Spatial coupling φ' slider that dynamically adjusts the edge thickness and runs a real-time coordinate descent energy minimization to update node states. (2) An 'Observation noise' slider that introduces synthetic noise to the observations and simulates inference on the hidden layer. (3) Clicking hidden nodes dynamically highlights their 'Markov Blanket' using colored torus halos (magenta for selection, gold for neighbors) and opens a detailed explanatory popup. (4) Clicking observed nodes and spatial edges acts as a guided step-through transition, invoking different narrative steps (goToStep) which animate sliders and reconfigure the 3D graph representation.
evaluation.faithfulness_analysis: The 3D model successfully captures the structure of the Markov Random Field grid with white base nodes and elevated observation nodes. However, it introduces several decorative elements not in the source, such as colored rings around nodes, blue-colored observation spheres, and interactive UI controls.
discrepancies: Colored highlight rings (yellow and pink) added to nodes.
Some observation nodes are colored blue instead of uniform gray.
Interactive sliders present in the screen space.
evaluation.faithfulness_improvement: Remove the colored rings, change all observation spheres to a uniform gray, and remove the UI sliders for a cleaner, more faithful match.
evaluation.label_quality_analysis: The source figure contains labels x1, x2, x3 for the hidden layer nodes and y1, y2, y3 for the observation nodes. The output includes all of these labels, but their positions are shifted due to the 3D rotation, and some labels like x2 and y2 overlap or collide with the colored highlighting rings, reducing readability.
evaluation.label_quality_improvement: Adjust the 3D anchor offsets of the labels (particularly x2 and y2) to prevent them from overlapping with the highlighting rings and connecting edges.
evaluation.concept_accuracy_analysis: Core concept: 2D Markov Random Fields (MRFs) with spatial dependencies and local observations, and the concept of the Markov blanket. User-visible claims: (1) Sliders for 'Spatial coupling φ' and 'Observation noise' correctly demonstrate how increasing neighbor consistency combats data corruption in MRFs. (2) Demo steps correctly identify the lower layer as hidden states (x) and the upper layer as observations (y). (3) The explanation of the Markov blanket for node x_22 correctly identifies its spatial neighbors and its associated observation node as its blanket, showing that they conditionally isolate it. All user-visible claims are accurate, educational, and mathematically precise.
evaluation.notes: The 3D MRF structure and interactive concept are excellently designed, but visual clutter, label misalignment, and overlapping text reduce faithfulness and legibility. Aligning labels to the correct back-row columns and refining the visual styling of observations and interactive halos will significantly improve the figure.

plan.contextChunk:
property: conditional on $x_2$, variable $x_3$ is independent of
variable $x_1$. The joint probability of all the variables shown here is
$p(x_1, x_2, x_3, y_1, y_2, y_3) =  \phi_{12}(x_1, x_2)  \phi_{23}(x_2, x_3)
\psi_{1}(y_1, x_1) \psi_{2}(y_2, x_2) \psi_{3}(y_3, x_3)$. Using
$p(a,b) = p(a \bigm | b) p(b)$, we can also write the probability of the
$x$ variables conditioned on the observations $y$,
$$p(x_1, x_2, x_3 \bigm | y_1, y_2, y_3) =  
\frac{1}{p(\mathbf{y})} \phi_{12}(x_1, x_2)  \phi_{23}(x_2, x_3) \psi_{1}(y_1, x_1) \psi_{2}(y_2, x_2) \psi_{3}(y_3, x_3).$$
For brevity, we write $p(\mathbf{y})$ for $p(y_1, y_2, y_3)$. Thus, to
form the conditional distribution, within a normalization factor, we
simply include the observed variable values into the joint probability.
For vision applications, we often use such Markov chain structures to
describe events over time.

To capture relationships over space, a two-dimensional (2D) structure is
useful, called a **Markov random field** (MRF) @Blake2011:

![Two-dimensional Markov random field.](figures/graphical_models/mrf.png){width="48%" #fig-leafs}

Then the joint probability over all the variables factorizes into this
product: 

$$p(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{y}) = 
\frac{1}{p(\mathbf{y})}
\prod_{(i,j)} \phi_{ij}(x_i, x_j) \prod_i \psi_i(x_i, y_i),$$
where the first product is over all spatial neighbors $i$ and $j$, and the second
product is over all nodes $i$.

An example of how Markov random field models are applied to images is
depicted in @fig-leafs, which show a small image region and its context
in the image (@fig-leafs [a]). @fig-leafs [b] shows an MRF with each
node corresponding to a pixel of the image region. The states of an MRF
can be indicator variables of image segment membership for each pixel.
The states of a hypothetical most-probable configuration of this MRF are
shown as the color of each node in this illustration.

:::{#fig-leafs layout-ncol="2"}
![](figures/graphical_models/leaf2.jpg){width=97% #fig-leafs-a}

![](figures/graphical_models/leaf1.jpg){width=100% #fig-leafs-b}

Fig (a) Image to be segmented and a local region of (a) marked in red.  (b) Visualization of an MRF of nodes corresponding to image pixels inside the marked region, with states indicating segment membership, for a hypothetical most probable configuration.
::: 

## Directed Graphical Models

In addition to undirected graphical models, another type of graphical
model is commonly used. **Directed graphical models** @Koller2009
describe factorizations of the joint probability into products of
conditional probability distributions. Each node in a directed graph
contributes a well-specified factor in the joint probability: the
probability of its variable, conditioned on all the variables originating
arrows pointing into it. So this graph

![A directed graphical model with three variables.](figures/graphical_models/directed.png){width="20%" #eq-directedjoint}

denotes the joint probability,

elements: 3x3 grid of hidden state nodes (x_ij) represented as spheres on a base plane, initially white
3x3 grid of observation nodes (y_ij) represented as gray/colored spheres elevated vertically above each x_ij
horizontal/lateral connecting cylinders (edges) between neighboring hidden state nodes (representing spatial potentials phi_ij)
vertical connecting cylinders between each hidden state node x_ij and its observation y_ij (representing local evidence potentials psi_i)
floating text labels 'x1', 'x2', 'x3' and 'y1', 'y2', 'y3' matching the back row of nodes in the original diagram
visual highlight ring/halo for indicating the Markov Blanket when a node is selected

interactions.label: Spatial Coupling (phi)
interactions.teaches: Higher spatial coupling forces neighboring hidden states to agree, smoothing out noisy local observations.

interactions.label: Observation Noise
interactions.teaches: Controls how noisy the upper observed nodes (y) are relative to the true underlying segmentation pattern.

interactions.label: Select Node
interactions.teaches: Click any hidden node x to highlight its Markov blanket—the set of nodes that, when observed, conditionally isolate it from the rest of the graph.

demo_steps.title: Hidden vs. Observed States
demo_steps.narration: In a Markov Random Field (MRF), the bottom layer contains the hidden true states (x), while the top layer contains the noisy observations (y). Each vertical link represents the likelihood potential psi_i connecting a pixel's observation to its actual state.

demo_steps.title: Denoising via Spatial Coupling
demo_steps.narration: When observation noise is high, the data layer (y) becomes corrupted. By turning up the spatial coupling (phi), the horizontal links force neighboring hidden nodes to coordinate, filtering out local noise and producing a clean, segmented region.

demo_steps.title: The Markov Blanket
demo_steps.narration: Click on the center node x2. Notice how its immediate neighbors (the adjacent x nodes and its own y node) light up. This is its Markov blanket: conditioned on these specific neighbors, this node is entirely independent of all other nodes in the network.

interactionPlan.camera_suggestion: An elevated 3D oblique angle looking down from the front-left, clearly showing the 2D grid floor, the vertical stems, and the floating observation layer.
interactionPlan.view_reasoning: (1) The grid lines of the MRF run horizontally left-to-right and diagonally receding into the page to the upper-right. (2) This receding diagonal structure implies a camera azimuth rotated away from a flat front view, specifically looking from the front-left (around -30 to -45 degrees). (3) The vertical offset of the y-nodes relative to the x-nodes is prominent, showing a clear height gap that requires a moderate, shallow elevation angle of around 20 to 25 degrees to avoid compressing the vertical stems too much.

camera_view.view_notes: Maintains the distinct spatial layered look of the MRF where x and y nodes do not overlap vertically from this viewpoint.

inline_constraints.default_view: Must match the original grid perspective, clean thin connection lines, and distinct shaded spheres.
inline_constraints.visible_ui: Position the coupling and noise sliders neatly in the upper-right corner without obscuring the grid.
inline_constraints.explainers: Hovering over a node displays its state probability or neighborhood potential equations.
inline_constraints.framing: The 3D grid must fit nicely inside the original figure footprint, leaving margin space for node labels on the back row.
inline_constraints.camera: Match the visual projection of the original hand-drawn graphical model so that elements align with the text's description.

interactionPlan.notes: Nodes should dynamically update their colors based on a real-time toy energy minimization (Gibbs sampling or simple belief propagation) running in the background when sliders are moved. True state is a binary segmentation (e.g., a diagonal edge of colored nodes); observations y are noisy versions of this.

evaluation.geometry_accuracy_analysis: The 3D grid layout closely replicates the source diagram. It uses real 3D primitives (spheres and cylinders) for all nodes and edges. The spatial relationships, vertical offsets, and boundary line extensions are preserved, although labels are slightly shifted.
evaluation.geometry_accuracy_improvement: Adjust the label offset values to align more cleanly with the top and right sides of the respective nodes as in the source.
evaluation.interactivity_usability_analysis: The developer built several interactive features: (1) A 'Coupling φ' slider and (2) an 'Observation Noise' slider. Both sliders are fully functional, triggering a real-time toy energy minimization algorithm (simulated inference) that updates the colors of the hidden and observed node layers in real time. (3) Node selection/clicking to reveal the Markov blanket, and (4) a step-by-step guided tutorial. However, interactions (3) and (4) are completely broken because they rely on undefined hallucinated functions: 'registerInteractive' and 'showPopup'. Clicking on nodes or attempting to trigger the demo steps will throw a ReferenceError in runtime.
evaluation.interactivity_usability_improvement: Implement a standard Three.js Raycaster to handle node clicking manually and replace the hallucinated 'showPopup' and 'registerInteractive' calls with standard DOM updates or floating HTML labels (using the provided addLabel function).
evaluation.faithfulness_analysis: The rendered output successfully captures the 3D grid layout of the MRF with white and grey spheres representing nodes. However, the camera angle is rotated, and the labeling sequence for both X and Y nodes is swapped or misplaced compared to the original left-to-right progression.

evaluation.concept_accuracy_analysis: Core concepts illustrated: (1) 2D Markov Random Field (MRF) structure for image segmentation/denoising (hidden states $x$ and observations $y$ connected by spatial and local evidence potentials), (2) The role of spatial coupling $\phi$ versus observation noise, and (3) The Markov blanket.
